newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Open Russian grain trade gives firms greater role.
newsitem.headline: Open Russian grain trade gives firms greater role.

text.p: Russian and Western grain traders, taking advantage of new opportunities to import grain privately to Russia, saw a growing market in 1996, and analysts on Tuesday said prospects for 1997 looked promising.

Until the early 1990s, Moscow authorities decided how much grain Russia would buy every year. But private traders have enjoyed a freer role in bringing grain to the Russian market after the government reduced its role.
"Every year commercial companies are becoming more important because the federal funds are buying so little (grain)," said Alexander Yukish, president of Russia's Grain Union.

But while the big traders are enjoying more flexibility, some of Russia's regions are finding the transition to market economy rules more trying, as they must now decide how much grain they need to secure food supplies.

"Moscow is not deciding these (grain) issues for the regions any more so they are having to decide them for themselves," said Daniel Day-Robinson of commodity consultancy firm Day-Robinson Ltd, a UK company contracted to the Know-How Fund. "This is putting some regions in extreme difficulties."
In 1996 total grain and flour imports to Russia nearly doubled to 5.1 million tonnes from 2.7 million in 1995, according to State Customs Committee figures.
The rise in imports was attributed to recent poor harvests.

"Imports rose during the 1995/96 crop year because this was one of the smallest harvests in the last 30 years," said specialist Andrei Sizov of the independent consultancy SovEcon Ltd. "Stocks also fell, which avoided even bigger imports."
In 1996 Russia's net grain harvest in 1996 was officially 69.3 million tonnes, the second smell return in a row.
Analysts were divided over the level of imports needed in 1997, but they agreed that commodity houses' slice of the business would be likely to rise.

Ties between trading firms and regional buyers are inevitably strengthening, meaning commercial enterprises have had to learn to cope with a wide range of partners rather than just one in Moscow, analysts said.

"The huge spread between different regions (and their grain needs) reflects a very fragmented approach to grain imports," Day-Robinson said. "Some regions are very forward thinking while others are not."

Last year Russia said it had quit the grain import business for good and that private traders would have to take up any slack -- a far cry from the 1970s, when the Soviet government was the world's largest grain importer.
Analysts said that while the new grain import system will turn out to be very different from the old one, many elements of the Soviet past could remain.
Some major Western trade houses involved in Russian grain business during the 1970s and 1980s have maintained their ties, and still number among the major players today.
"The nomenclature of the old system is still there, and those traders have maintained their links," said one analyst.
Investment in farming infrastructure across Russia could eventually flow through these companies in the form of joint ventures, analysts said.
Smaller commodity firms may find it tough to break into the newly-fragmented grain import business, mainly because of high risks involved in investing in Russia, they added.
